# Analysis plan

This chapter is written before any outcome is examined. Changes after that
point are logged in the decision record with a reason. It was revised
after plan review, before any data were seen (D-013 to D-017).

## Population and unit of analysis

All randomized patients, analysed in the group they were randomized to
(intention to treat). Patients with a sore throat before surgery
(`preOp_pain`) are kept. The unit of analysis is the patient (D-005).

## Outcomes

All outcomes are any sore throat at rest, defined as a score above zero on
the zero-to-ten scale.

- **Primary:** thirty minutes after PACU arrival (`pacu30min_throatPain`;
  D-001).
- **Secondary:** ninety minutes after PACU arrival
  (`pacu90min_throatPain`), four hours after surgery
  (`postOp4hour_throatPain`) and the first postoperative morning
  (`pod1am_throatPain`; D-002).

Cough is not analysed (D-004). Swallowing pain is an open question for the
client (Chapter 1).

## Estimands

Every comparison is licorice against sugar water in all randomized
patients; because the analyses are complete case, this holds only if
missing outcomes are missing completely at random (see Missing data). The
odds ratios that answer the client's questions are
population-averaged (marginal): they compare the odds of sore throat had
everyone received licorice with the odds had everyone received sugar water
(D-002). Each odds ratio is reported with the proportion with any sore
throat in each arm and the risk difference, because the odds ratio
overstates the relative risk when the outcome is common (D-006).

| Question | Population | Outcome | Summary measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary: did it reduce sore throat? | All randomized | Any sore throat at rest, thirty minutes after PACU arrival | Marginal odds ratio; risk difference |
| Secondary: does it last? | All randomized | The same outcome at each later assessment | Marginal odds ratio and risk difference at each assessment |
| Summary across time (does not answer "does it last") | All randomized | The same outcome at all four assessments | Common marginal odds ratio, assuming one common effect |
| Supporting: patient-level effect | All randomized | The same outcome at all four assessments | Common conditional odds ratio (mixed model) |
| Sensitivity: covariate adjustment | All randomized | Primary outcome | Covariate-conditional odds ratio |

Two of these odds ratios are conditional, and both are reported only
beside the marginal estimate with a label saying so. The mixed-model odds
ratio compares the odds for the same patient under licorice and under
sugar water; it is further from one than the marginal odds ratio whenever
patients differ in their underlying risk, even with no change in the
treatment effect (D-008). The adjusted odds ratio compares patients with
the same covariate values; it differs from the unadjusted one even when
the arms are perfectly balanced, for the same reason (odds ratios are
non-collapsible), so a difference is not by itself evidence of
confounding (D-009).

**Does it last?** Durability is judged from the per-time odds ratios,
risk differences and their 95% CIs, read together. There is no formal
test across time points. A non-significant result at a later assessment
is not evidence that the effect wore off: it means the data cannot rule
out no effect at that time, and the CI shows which effects remain
plausible (D-003, D-013).

**The common odds ratio** assumes one treatment effect shared by all four
assessments, including the primary one at thirty minutes. If the effect
changes over time, it is a weighted average that leans toward the early,
better-observed assessments. It is a summary only and does not answer
"does it last"; the per-time estimates do. The same holds for the
mixed-model common odds ratio (D-014).

## Models

- **Primary and each assessment.** Unadjusted logistic regression of any
  sore throat on treatment, fitted separately at each assessment with all
  patients observed at that assessment. With treatment as the only term,
  its odds ratio is the marginal odds ratio. The risk difference is the
  difference in observed proportions, with a Wald 95% CI (D-006, D-007).
- **Common marginal odds ratio.** A generalized estimating equation (GEE)
  with a logit link, treatment and assessment (as a factor) as terms, an
  exchangeable working correlation within patient and robust (sandwich)
  standard errors, fitted with `geepack` (D-007). There is no
  treatment-by-assessment term, so the model assumes one common effect
  (D-014).
- **Common conditional odds ratio.** A logistic mixed model with the same
  terms and a random intercept for patient, fitted with `lme4`. Labeled as
  patient-level in every table and sentence where it appears (D-008).
- **Adjusted sensitivity analysis.** Logistic regression of the primary
  outcome on treatment, sex, age, BMI, ASA status, smoking and surgery
  size, plus preoperative sore throat unless fewer than ten patients have
  it (counted from baseline data only). Age and BMI enter as linear terms;
  ASA status, smoking and surgery size as factors. Any covariate category
  with fewer than ten patients is merged into its neighbour, decided from
  baseline counts only. Mallampati class is not included: it acts through
  intubation difficulty, which is not measured, and leaving it out keeps
  the model small. The adjusted odds ratio is conditional on the
  covariates (D-009, D-011, D-016).

All CIs are Wald 95% CIs (D-007). Warnings from any fit are reported as
findings, not suppressed.

## Missing data

There is no variable for "not assessable"; any missing score is treated
as missing. Each analysis uses the patients observed at that assessment
(complete case). The GEE and the mixed model use every observed assessment
for each patient (D-010). The complete-case analyses assume outcomes are
missing completely at random (MCAR) (D-015).

For the primary outcome, best- and worst-case bounds: refit the primary
model with every missing outcome in the licorice arm set to no sore throat
and every missing outcome in the sugar-water arm set to sore throat (best
case for licorice), then the reverse (worst case). If the primary
conclusion holds at both bounds, the missing patients cannot change it.

Bounds are computed for the primary outcome only (D-010, D-015).

The number of patients missing each outcome, by arm, is reported in the
data chapter (D-012). If more than five percent of patients are missing
the outcome at any assessment, the missing-data approach is revisited
before any model is fitted, with a decision entry (D-015).

## Verification before trusting a model

Each model function must recover a known effect from simulated data with
the same structure before it is run on the study data
(`tests/testthat/test-models.R`). For the GEE and the mixed model, the
simulation draws correlated repeated outcomes per patient, and each model
must recover its own estimand: the marginal and the conditional odds
ratio differ for the same simulated data. When outcomes are simulated
from a random-intercept model, the true marginal odds ratio is not a model
parameter; it is computed by numerical integration over the
random-intercept distribution (D-017).

The risk-difference Wald CI gets a known-answer test (D-017).

*Added after the plan was locked at `plan-v1`, before any data were seen
(D-018):* the recovery test for the common odds ratio, from both the GEE
and the mixed model, simulates a treatment effect that is constant over
time, since only then does the common odds ratio have a single true value.
The best- and worst-case bounds procedure gets a known-answer test.

## Reporting

Effect sizes with 95% CI; p-values to three decimals. There is no
multiplicity adjustment: there is one primary comparison, and the
secondary analyses are descriptive (D-003). The marginal odds ratios and
risk differences are the reported effects; conditional odds ratios always
appear labeled, next to the marginal estimate.
